title: SqueezeBench: Saturation-Resilient Evaluation of Mathematical Capability
title_zh: SqueezeBench：对数学能力饱和度的鲁棒性评估

paragraphs.en: AI systems are making rapid progress in mathematics, but this progress is hard to measure. Benchmarks of solved problems saturate, and in benchmarks of open problems each problem can be resolved for the first time only once. We present SqueezeBench , a benchmark that is resilient to saturation: a success raises the bar instead of removing the problem. Each problem fixes an integer function f ⁡ ( n ) f(n) whose values are known only for small n n , and the benchmark keeps a lower and an upper record on it. A record is a computable Lean function with a machine-checked proof that it bounds f f . A submission proposes a new function and proves that it bounds f f , that it is no worse than the current record at any n n , and that it is strictly better at some n n . Once accepted, it becomes the record that the next submission has to beat. The system thus chooses the bound as well as its proof, and it may improve the record at a single n n or improve its growth rate. At every n n , the gap between the two records shows how far the certified bounds are from determining f ⁡ ( n ) f(n) . Every proof is checked by two independent Lean kernels, so no referee needs to check the mathematics. The checks also reject a function that computes f f by exhaustive search at small n n , and a maintainer only reads the submitter’s report and looks for such a search at larger n n . We release ten problems from extremal combinatorics with twenty proved initial records, together with the admission tools. As a baseline, agents based on a frontier language model, with at most one hour per record, had 82 submissions accepted and improved every record, without going beyond the published literature. Agents based on two newer models then started from these records, had 60 more submissions accepted and improved 19 of the 20 records again. For eight of the ten problems, at least one record is still asymptotically behind the best published bound.

paragraphs.en: This progress is hard to measure. A benchmark of solved problems has a maximum score, and as the best systems approach it, their scores can no longer be told apart ( Akhtar et al., 2026 ) . Four systems have reported solving all 672 problems of PutnamBench ( Tsoukalas et al., 2024 ; PutnamBench maintainers, 2026 ) , and the maintainers of FrontierMath consider its hardest tier saturated ( Stewart, 2026 ) . The answers of such benchmarks are often public, so they may also end up in the training data of the systems they evaluate. Benchmarks of open problems, such as FrontierMath Erdős ( Adamczewski and Bloom, 2026 ) , avoid known answers, but each problem yields at most one first resolution. After that, its solution is public, and a later system that solves it may be reproducing a published solution, so the set of informative problems shrinks as the systems improve. Their scores count resolved problems, and intermediate progress, such as a better bound, earns little or no credit. In both kinds of benchmark the statement to be proved is given, and the system is not asked to find it. Record archives such as EinsteinArena ( Bianchi et al., 2026 ) and Optimization Constants in Mathematics ( Davis et al., 2026 ) keep improvable records, but a record there is a number for a fixed problem, checked by running a witness or by citing a paper, and no kernel checks a bound’s proof.

paragraphs.en: Each accepted submission is stored with its author and date. At any time each record has a holder, and the record history of a problem shows who held which bound, when, and by how much each submission moved it. This history is the leaderboard. We do not reduce it to a single score, since progress on twenty records, each a function of n n , has many dimensions. To compare systems in a controlled way, we start each of them from the same snapshot of records with the same budget and compare the records they reach, value by value, not the number of accepted submissions. paragraphs.en: As part of our benchmark, we formalize ten problems in the field of extremal combinatorics. This branch of mathematics studies how large or how small a finite object can be, subject to certain conditions. For instance, as we will further explain in Section 4.2 , SqueezeBench includes the Golomb ruler problem ( Bloom and Golomb, 1977 ) , which asks the following question: for every natural number n n , what is the smallest possible length of a set of n n integers whose pairwise differences are all distinct, where the length is the difference between the largest and the smallest integer? In other words, these are rulers with n n marks that measure no distance twice. For small values of n n , one could even solve this problem by hand: for n = 3 n=3 , the ruler { 0 , 1 , 3 } \{0,1,3\} has length 3, but no ruler of length 2 exists, since { 0 , 1 , 2 } \{0,1,2\} measures the distance 1 twice. Thus, the smallest possible length is 3. For n = 4 n=4 , one can find rulers of length 6, such as { 0 , 1 , 4 , 6 } \{0,1,4,6\} , but not of length 5, since the six pairwise differences would be distinct positive integers no larger than 5. Therefore, the shortest ruler has length 6. However, as the value of n n increases, finding such shortest rulers becomes intractable, since there are ( L − 1 n − 2 ) \binom{L-1}{n-2} candidate rulers of length L L . Although there is no known solution for the Golomb ruler problem for all possible values of n n , researchers have proved upper and lower bounds on these numbers ( Singer, 1938 ; Erdős and Turán, 1941 ; Lindström, 1969 ) . This problem is typical of the problems in SqueezeBench . For each of them, the exact answer is known only for a small number of values of the parameter, or for special families of them, and no closed formula is known for the general case. In contrast, we consider bounds that are explicit: each has to be a computable function that can be evaluated at every value of the parameter. They can be closed formulas, tables or programs that build explicit constructions. The task is to narrow the gap between these known functions and the unknown answer. Note that our requirement on bounds is stronger than what the literature typically provides, where the best bounds are often asymptotic, with unspecified constants or valid only for sufficiently large values.
paragraphs.zh: 作为我们基准测试的一部分，我们将极值组合学领域的十个问题形式化。 这一数学分支研究在特定条件下，有限对象可以变得多大或多小。 例如，正如我们将在第 4.2 节中进一步解释的，SqueezeBench 包含了戈洛姆尺问题（Bloom 和 Golomb，1977），该问题提出如下疑问：对于每个自然数 n，由 n 个整数组成的集合，若其中任意两个数的差值均不相同，其可能的最小长度是多少？这里的“长度”指的是最大整数与最小整数之差。 换言之，这些是带有 n 个刻度的尺子，且不会重复测量任何距离。 对于较小的 n 值，这个问题甚至可以通过手工解决：当 n = 3 时，尺子 {0, 1, 3} 的长度为 3，但不存在长度为 2 的尺子，因为 {0, 1, 2} 会重复测量距离 1。 因此，可能的最小长度是 3。 对于 n = 4，可以找到长度为 6 的尺子，例如 {0, 1, 4, 6}，但无法找到长度为 5 的尺子，因为六个两两之差必须是不超过 5 的不同正整数。 因此，最短的尺子长度为 6。 然而，随着 n 值的增大，寻找这样的最短尺子变得难以处理，因为长度为 L 的候选尺子有 $\binom{L-1}{n-2}$ 种。 尽管目前尚未找到适用于所有可能 n 值的戈洛姆尺问题的解法，但研究人员已经证明了这些数值的上下界（Singer，1938；Erdős 和 Turán，1941；Lindström，1969）。 这个问题是 SqueezeBench 中典型问题的代表。 对于这些问题中的每一个，其精确解仅在少数参数值或特定参数族的情况下已知，而一般情况下的闭式公式尚未被发现。 相比之下，我们考虑的是显式的界：每个界都必须是一个可计算的函数，并且能够在参数的每个取值上进行计算。 这些界可以是闭式公式、表格，或是能够构建显式构造的程序。 任务在于缩小这些已知函数与未知答案之间的差距。 请注意，我们对界的要求比文献中通常提供的更强：文献中的最佳界往往是渐近性的，包含未指定的常数，或仅对足够大的值有效。

sents.en: This problem is typical of the problems in SqueezeBench .

sents.en: For each of them, the exact answer is known only for a small number of values of the parameter, or for special families of them, and no closed formula is known for the general case.

sents.en: In contrast, we consider bounds that are explicit: each has to be a computable function that can be evaluated at every value of the parameter.

sents.en: The task is to narrow the gap between these known functions and the unknown answer.

sents.en: Note that our requirement on bounds is stronger than what the literature typically provides, where the best bounds are often asymptotic, with unspecified constants or valid only for sufficiently large values.

paragraphs.en: We have formalized each problem in Lean 4, building on its mathematical library, Mathlib ( The mathlib Community, 2020 ) . The answer to each problem is a function f : ℕ → ℕ f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} , where f ⁡ ( n ) f(n) is the optimal value for the parameter n n . In Lean, f f is defined by its combinatorial meaning, typically as a maximum or minimum over a finite set, but no closed form for f f is known. This is what makes the benchmark resilient to saturation: if f f had a closed form, the lower and upper bounds could meet at every n n , and the problem would be solved. This could eventually happen—and we would welcome a submission that settles an open problem—but we select problems for which it is not expected soon. Each problem also fixes a smallest parameter value n min n_{\min} , in practice 1, 2 or 3, below which f f is set to 0 0 . Some definitions degenerate at such small values, and pinning them lets a bound be stated for every n n without side conditions.

paragraphs.en: A submission must be checked without trusting the person who wrote it. For this, we use Comparator ( Lean FRO, 2026a ) , a tool from the Lean FRO for judging Lean proofs, which is also used by other projects such as lean-eval ( Lean FRO, 2026b ) and Palomar ( Palomar, 2026 ) . Comparator takes a trusted challenge , which states theorems with their proofs left as sorry and may leave some definitions open, and an untrusted solution , which fills them in. It checks that the solution proves exactly the statements of the challenge and uses no axioms beyond a given list. We allow only the three standard axioms propext , Quot.sound and Classical.choice , so sorry and native_decide are rejected. It then checks the proofs with the Lean kernel and, in our setup, also with nanoda ( Bailey, 2026 ) , an independent implementation of the kernel. Our design follows this interface. For every new version of a record, SqueezeBench provides a Challenge : a trusted Lean file in which the new record definition is left open, and valid , improves and strict are stated in terms of f f and the current record. The solution is split into two Lean files: Def.lean defines the new function, and Proof.lean imports it and proves the three theorems. The split matters because the next Challenge imports Def.lean to refer to this record, which makes that file trusted; keeping the proofs out of it keeps the trusted part small. Two more files complete the submission: metadata.toml gives the author name and the witness n 0 n_{0} , and REPORT.md explains how the bound and its proofs were obtained and the setup used, including the models or agents. SqueezeBench is hosted in a public GitHub repository, and a submission is a pull request that adds these four files.

paragraphs.en: SqueezeBench lies between mathematical reasoning benchmarks, archives of best known results and formal theorem proving, and Table 1 compares it with benchmarks and archives.
paragraphs.zh: SqueezeBench 介于数学推理基准测试、已知最佳结果档案库和形式化定理证明之间，表 1 将其与各类基准测试和档案库进行了比较。

paragraphs.en: Benchmarks of solved problems, such as miniF2F ( Zheng et al., 2022 ) and ProofNet ( Azerbayev et al., 2023 ) , hold out known answers, which can leak into training data, and they saturate. Benchmarks of open problems avoid known answers. FrontierMath Erdős ( Adamczewski and Bloom, 2026 ) asks for Lean proofs or disproofs of 68 Erdős problems, and Formal Conjectures ( Firsching et al., 2026 ) collects open conjectures from many areas, such as number theory and spectral theory, and HorizonMath ( Wang et al., 2026 ) scores programs that compute values for open problems against fixed baselines.
paragraphs.zh: 已解决问题的基准测试，例如 miniF2F（Zheng 等人，2022）和 ProofNet（Azerbayev 等人，2023），会保留已知答案，而这些答案可能会泄露到训练数据中，并且这些测试最终会达到饱和。 开放问题的基准测试则避免了使用已知答案。 FrontierMath Erdős（Adamczewski 和 Bloom，2026）要求为 68 个 Erdős 问题提供 Lean 证明或反证；Formal Conjectures（Firsching 等人，2026）收集了来自数论和谱理论等多个领域的开放猜想；而 HorizonMath（Wang 等人，2026）则通过计算开放问题的数值结果，并与固定的基准线进行比较来对程序进行评分。

paragraphs.en: Archives of best known results track moving targets, such as the surveys of small Ramsey numbers ( Radziszowski, 2026 ) and of cages ( Exoo and Jajcay, 2013 ) . Their updates rest on human checking, and each covers its own problems. Newer collections gather many problems in one place, such as Leaps in Bounds (LoB) ( Munro, 2026 ) , FrontierShift ( AItonomy Foundation, 2026 ) and Optimization Constants in Mathematics ( Davis et al., 2026 ) , which Terence Tao started 1 1 1 https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/01/22/a-crowdsourced-repository-for-optimization-constants/ . They are updated semi-automatically and accept a claim backed by a citation, without a formal proof. FunSearch ( Romera-Paredes et al., 2024 ) , AlphaEvolve ( Novikov et al., 2025 ) and PatternBoost ( Charton et al., 2024 ) find constructions by search and check each with a program; FunSearch’s cap sets of growth 2.2202 2.2202 exceed our lower record. These systems are potential submitters, not competitors, since a construction enters the benchmark once proved in Lean. SqueezeBench is not a search method: it adds a Lean proof valid at every n n and keeps a lower and an upper record.

paragraphs.en: Progress on such problems rarely comes as a single proof. In combinatorics in particular, the bounds on an extremal function are tightened step by step by many researchers, and even an improvement at a single value can matter. A benchmark that asks for a proof of a fixed statement or for a better scalar cannot credit such steps on a function whose values are unknown, and a single proof of a conjecture does not credit the earlier work it builds on.
paragraphs.zh: 这类问题的进展很少以单一证明的形式出现。 尤其是在组合数学领域，许多研究者会逐步收紧极值函数的界限，即使仅在一个特定数值上的改进也可能具有重要意义。 一个要求对固定命题进行证明或寻求更优标量的基准测试，无法对某个未知函数值的改进步骤给予认可；而一个猜想的单一证明也无法体现其所依赖的早期工作。

paragraphs.en: The ten problems come from three areas of extremal combinatorics ( Table 2 ): additive combinatorics (cap sets, Roth numbers, the Ruzsa–Szemerédi problem and Golomb rulers), extremal graph theory (graphs without a 4-cycle, graphs without cycles of length 3 or 4, and subgraphs of the hypercube without a 4-cycle), and Ramsey theory (the diagonal Ramsey numbers R ⁡ ( n , n ) R(n,n) , the Ramsey numbers R ⁡ ( 3 , k ) R(3,k) and the Schur numbers). Each problem has a single integer parameter, and its exact values are known only up to a small size, for example n ≤ 4 n\leq 4 for R ⁡ ( n , n ) R(n,n) , k ≤ 5 k\leq 5 for the Schur numbers, n ≤ 6 n\leq 6 for cap sets and for the hypercube, and n ≤ 28 n\leq 28 for Golomb rulers.

paragraphs.en: Every one of the twenty records improved on its seed. In the first phase, the Opus 5 agents had 82 submissions accepted in 18.9 hours, and sixteen of the twenty tracks were stopped by the time limit rather than by two idle sessions. In the second phase, the Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 agents had 60 more submissions accepted and improved 19 of the 20 records again. Table 2 lists the standing records: ten match the leading term or the growth rate of the best published bound, one matches the best elementary bound, and nine are asymptotically behind. Nearly all accepted proofs are general arguments, such as explicit algebraic constructions, products of smaller constructions, and counting arguments; decide only checks explicit witnesses. Gate 6 was added during the second phase, and it rejected one record that had passed the earlier checks in an agent’s copy of the repository but was not yet merged. The first formalization of the Ellenberg–Gijswijt bound computed its values by a recursion over lists and exceeded the budget at every n n from 59 to 100, so the next submitter could not have evaluated it. The agent resubmitted the bound with a computation that needs fewer than 100 heartbeats per n n . One record may go beyond the literature at concrete values. For the Ruzsa–Szemerédi problem, a Fable 5.1 agent localized a counting argument of Fox et al. (2017) , suggested by the second model it consulted, and combined it with the degree bounds of earlier versions. The resulting upper record gives f ⁡ ( 50 ) ≤ 140 f(50)\leq 140 and f ⁡ ( 100 ) ≤ 529 f(100)\leq 529 , where the best bounds we could derive from the literature are 144 and 566. We found no published bound that gives these values; asymptotically, the record is still far from the o ⁡ ( n 2 ) o(n^{2}) bound of the triangle removal lemma.

paragraphs.en: Apart from possibly the Ruzsa–Szemerédi record, no record goes beyond the published literature. Both records match the leading term of the best published bounds only for C 4 C_{4} -free graphs and Golomb rulers; for the other eight problems at least one record stays behind ( Table 2 ). For example, the upper record for the diagonal Ramsey numbers gives R ⁡ ( 5 , 5 ) ≤ 58 R(5,5)\leq 58 , while the published bound is 46 ( Radziszowski, 2026 ) . Some of the best bounds rest on results that Mathlib lacks, or whose explicit constants are far too weak at these n n , such as the triangle removal lemma. Others were obtained by computer, and there the two directions differ. A construction found by a search comes with a witness, which is cheap to check once it is published: the agents imported the best known Golomb rulers up to 100 marks and a Schur coloring that shows S ⁡ ( 7 ) ≥ 1696 S(7)\geq 1696 . An impossibility result found by an exhaustive search has no short certificate and exceeds the computation budget, as for f ⁡ ( 28 ) = 585 f(28)=585 , so it can enter a record only through an argument that is not known yet. Published but unformalized bounds leave room for further submissions. Beyond them, the records reach values of f f that nobody knows, and formalizing the literature alone cannot saturate the benchmark.

paragraphs.en: SqueezeBench measures mathematical progress by records rather than by solved statements. A record is a computable function with a proof that it bounds f f , and a submission replaces it only by proving that it is valid, no worse at any n n and better at some n n , checked by two kernels against statements fixed in advance. In our evaluation the records left by one system became the starting point of the next. After 82 accepted submissions of the baseline, agents based on newer models had 60 more accepted and improved 19 of the 20 records again, and eight of the ten problems still have a record behind the literature. The record history is the leaderboard.
paragraphs.zh: SqueezeBench 通过记录而非已解决的陈述来衡量数学进展。 记录是一个可计算函数，并附有证明表明它界定了 f f；提交内容只需通过证明其有效性、在任何 n n 处表现不差且在某些 n n 处更优即可替代该记录，这一过程由两个内核针对预先固定的陈述进行验证。 在我们的评估中，一个系统留下的记录成为了下一个系统的起点。 在基准模型提交了 82 次有效提交后，基于更新模型的智能体又获得了 60 次有效提交，并再次改进了 20 个记录中的 19 个；十个问题中仍有八个的记录落后于文献水平。 记录历史就是排行榜。

paragraphs.en: The benchmark has limits. Its ten problems come from one area of mathematics and have one parameter each. Future work will add problems with several parameters and admit proofs that rely on a verified checker for SAT certificates, marked as such, as a route for these bounds. SqueezeBench is open to submissions from people and AI systems alike.

paragraphs.en: To add a new problem to SqueezeBench , the following steps must be followed.
paragraphs.zh: 要向 SqueezeBench 添加新问题，必须遵循以下步骤。

paragraphs.en:
Define the problem. Problems/

/Def.lean defines n min n_{\min} and f f by its combinatorial meaning, pinned to 0 0 below n min n_{\min} , reusing a definition from Mathlib where one exists. It also provides, for each direction, a lemma that reduces a bound to its combinatorial content, such as the existence of a witness of a given size. Where f f can be evaluated, its smallest values are checked by decide on every build. If f f is a least element, the file also proves that the set is nonempty; without this, no lower record can be proved.
paragraphs.zh:
定义问题。 Problems/
